_meta.criterion: An ingredient is 'executable' if a student committing its failure_mode produces a characteristic wrong VALUE that can be computed from the problem and placed in an answer option; 'interpretation' if the value computed is correct but is misread, mislabelled, or unexplainable; 'meta' if the ingredient is a strategy, verification, or self-monitoring skill that yields no value at all.
_meta.method: Hand-classified by reading each failure_mode; no LLM call. Judged by the mechanism described, not by whether the wording contains digits. Under-claiming preferred: genuinely torn entries are marked non-executable with confidence 'low' and the tension recorded in 'note'.

field_semantics.failure_signature: executable only; omission = required step skipped, substitution = wrong operation/value used in place of the right one, sequencing = correct steps in the wrong order, overgeneralized_rule = valid rule applied outside its domain
field_semantics.symbolically_tractable: executable only; true if a SymPy-style engine could compute the wrong value from an algebraic problem statement, false if it needs diagram/geometry/chart reading or natural-language judgement

candidates.failure_mode: Students treat numerator and denominator as two separate unrelated numbers rather than as a ratio describing parts of a single whole

candidates.failure_mode: Students add or subtract the same number from both top and bottom instead of multiplying, producing non-equivalent fractions

candidates.failure_mode: Students add numerators and denominators separately: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 instead of the correct 5/6
candidates.note: Adds numerators and denominators componentwise: a/b + c/d -> (a+c)/(b+d).

candidates.failure_mode: Students order decimals by digit count not value: concluding 0.25 is greater than 0.7 because 25 is greater than 7
candidates.note: Compares decimals as if the digit strings were integers, so it picks the wrong element in an ordering or comparison.

candidates.failure_mode: Students write 3/4 as 0.34 or 3.4 by simply concatenating digits without performing the division

candidates.failure_mode: Students cannot identify which quantity goes in the denominator when setting up a unit rate from a word problem

candidates.failure_mode: Students apply cross multiplication to non-proportion situations or forget it only applies when exactly two fractions are set equal

candidates.failure_mode: Students evaluate strictly left-to-right regardless of operation type, computing 2 + 3 times 4 as 20 instead of 14

candidates.failure_mode: Students distribute into parentheses before evaluating inside them: 2(3+4) computed as 6+4 = 10 instead of 2 times 7 = 14
candidates.note: Distributes into the parentheses before evaluating inside them: 2(3+4) -> 6+4 = 10.

candidates.failure_mode: Students compute 2x squared as (2x) squared when x=3, getting 36 instead of the correct 2 times 9 = 18

candidates.failure_mode: Students chain computations through equals signs: writing 5+3=8+2=10, using equals as meaning the answer so far is

candidates.failure_mode: Students skip verification entirely, missing sign errors or arithmetic mistakes that substitution would immediately catch

candidates.failure_mode: Students try to determine slope from a single point alone or confuse which point goes in which position of the slope formula

candidates.failure_mode: Students compute trig values of angles like 150 or 225 degrees from scratch instead of using the reference angle and adjusting only the sign

candidates.failure_mode: Students differentiate products as f-prime times g-prime, incorrectly treating differentiation as distributing over multiplication

candidates.failure_mode: Students solve each part of a compound inequality separately and present two disconnected answers instead of the intersection as one interval

candidates.failure_mode: Students subtract equations when they should add, or forget to multiply the entire equation (not just one term) before adding

candidates.failure_mode: Students interpret a large standard deviation as meaning the data is wrong rather than understanding it describes natural variability in the dataset

candidates.failure_mode: Students do arithmetic correctly but use the wrong category value from the chart or fail to combine the requested categories.

candidates.failure_mode: Students use n instead of (n minus 1) as the multiplier, causing every term to be off by one position

candidates.failure_mode: Students add terms one by one instead of using the formula, or confuse the formula for arithmetic series with the geometric series formula

candidates.failure_mode: Students cancel terms rather than factors: in (x squared + 2x)/(x + 2) they cancel the x squared and the 2 instead of factoring x out first
candidates.note: Cancels matching terms rather than factors, e.g. cancelling x^2 and 2 in (x^2+2x)/(x+2).

candidates.failure_mode: Students multiply the denominators together instead of finding the LCD, creating unnecessarily complex expressions that are harder to simplify
candidates.note: Multiplying denominators instead of using the LCD yields an unsimplified but still correct expression; the cost is effort, not accuracy.

candidates.failure_mode: Students simplify correctly but forget to state the excluded values, not realizing cancellation hides them from the simplified form
candidates.note: Omits the excluded values that cancellation hides, so the reported domain restriction set is a specific incomplete one.

candidates.failure_mode: Students treat i as a variable like x, not recognizing that i squared has a specific value of negative-1 and must be simplified
candidates.note: Leaves i^2 unsimplified as if i were a variable, so the result keeps an i^2 term instead of -1.

candidates.failure_mode: Students compute i to the large powers by multiplying step by step for many steps instead of using the period-4 pattern
candidates.note: Stepwise multiplication is slow but arrives at the correct power of i; the missing period-4 shortcut costs time only.

candidates.failure_mode: Students multiply complex numbers using FOIL correctly but forget to apply i squared = negative-1 to the last term, leaving i squared in the answer
candidates.note: Expands correctly but omits the i^2 = -1 substitution, so the real part is off by that term.

candidates.failure_mode: Students swap the sin and cos components, assigning cos to the vertical and sin to the horizontal
candidates.note: Assigns cos to the vertical and sin to the horizontal, swapping the two components.

candidates.failure_mode: Students add magnitudes of vectors instead of components, getting a scalar instead of a new vector
candidates.note: Adds magnitudes instead of components, giving a scalar sum rather than the resultant magnitude.

candidates.failure_mode: Students compute dot products correctly but report the scalar result as a vector, or cannot interpret a zero dot product as perpendicularity
candidates.note: The dot product is computed correctly; only its scalar nature and the perpendicularity reading are misstated.

candidates.failure_mode: Students attempt to multiply matrices in any order without checking dimension compatibility, producing meaningless results
candidates.note: Omits the dimension-compatibility check and asserts a product that is undefined, a selectable wrong answer.

candidates.failure_mode: Students reverse the order of matrix multiplication when it is more convenient, not realizing this gives a completely different result
candidates.note: Computes BA where AB is required, giving a different and specific matrix.

candidates.failure_mode: Students apply a row operation to only one element in the row instead of all elements across the entire row
candidates.note: Applies the row operation to one entry instead of the whole row, giving a specific wrong matrix.

candidates.failure_mode: Students classify an ellipse as a circle when they see both x squared and y squared, missing that unequal coefficients make it an ellipse
candidates.note: Classifies any x^2 + y^2 equation as a circle, ignoring unequal coefficients that make it an ellipse.

candidates.failure_mode: Students add the completing-the-square constant to one side only, forgetting to add it to the other side of the equation as well
candidates.note: Adds the completing constant to one side only, shifting the resulting radius/constant by that amount.

candidates.failure_mode: Students read center as (negative-h, negative-k) from (x-h) and (y-k), getting the signs backwards
candidates.note: Reads the centre as (-h,-k) from (x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2, giving sign-flipped coordinates.

candidates.failure_mode: Students assign probabilities that sum to more or less than 1, not recognizing this violates the fundamental requirement
candidates.note: Omits the sum-to-1 constraint, so an invalid distribution (or a probability derived from one) is offered as the answer.

candidates.failure_mode: Students apply the 68-95-99.7 percentages to non-symmetric ranges without adjusting: computing P(mu to mu + sigma) as 68% instead of 34%
candidates.note: Applies the full 68% to a one-sided range that should be 34%.

candidates.failure_mode: Students compute z-scores correctly but then look up the wrong tail in the z-table, finding P(Z less than z) when the problem asks for P(Z greater than z)
candidates.note: Reads the opposite tail of the z-table, returning 1 - p instead of p.

candidates.failure_mode: Students set f equal to zero instead of f-prime equal to zero, finding x-intercepts instead of critical points
candidates.note: Solves f(x) = 0 instead of f'(x) = 0, returning x-intercepts as critical points.

candidates.failure_mode: Students evaluate f-prime at the critical point itself (getting zero) instead of on either side of it to determine sign changes
candidates.note: Evaluates f' at the critical point itself rather than on either side, so the extremum is classified wrongly.

candidates.failure_mode: Students confuse concave up with maximum — they think the bowl shape of concave up means it is at the top
candidates.note: Reads concave up as a maximum, returning the wrong extremum classification.

candidates.failure_mode: Students differentiate the objective function with multiple variables without first using the constraint to eliminate one variable
candidates.note: Differentiates the multivariable objective without first substituting the constraint, yielding a specific wrong optimum.

candidates.failure_mode: Students forget the plus-C constant of integration for indefinite integrals, losing the family of solutions
candidates.note: Omits the +C, so the reported indefinite integral is the single-antiderivative form.

candidates.failure_mode: Students compute the definite integral without recognizing that regions below the x-axis contribute negative area, getting incorrect total areas
candidates.note: Omits the sign handling below the axis, so signed integral and total area are conflated into a specific wrong number.

candidates.failure_mode: Students forget to subtract F(a) and report only F(b), missing the subtraction entirely
candidates.note: Reports F(b) without subtracting F(a).

candidates.failure_mode: Students add plus-C to definite integrals or omit it from indefinite integrals — they do not distinguish which type they are computing
candidates.note: Attaches +C to a definite integral or drops it from an indefinite one, giving the wrong answer form.

candidates.failure_mode: Students integrate only the upper function without subtracting the lower, computing the area between the upper function and the x-axis instead of between the two curves
candidates.note: Integrates the upper curve alone, omitting the lower-curve subtraction.

candidates.failure_mode: Students confuse net change with total distance traveled — for motion problems they do not recognize that negative velocity means the object moved backward
candidates.note: Reports the signed net change where total distance is asked (or vice versa), two different computable numbers.

candidates.failure_mode: Students expect the sample mean to exactly equal the population mean and interpret any difference as evidence the sample is wrong
candidates.note: The sample statistic is computed correctly; the failure is expecting it to match the parameter exactly.

candidates.failure_mode: Students write the alternative hypothesis as the status quo and the null as the new claim, reversing the logical structure of hypothesis testing
candidates.note: Swaps null and alternative, so the stated hypothesis pair is a specific wrong option; the swap needs natural-language reading of the claim.

candidates.failure_mode: Students interpret p = 0.03 as meaning there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, when it actually means there is a 3% chance of getting data this extreme if the null were true
candidates.note: The p-value is correct; the error is reading it as P(null is true) rather than a wrong number.

candidates.failure_mode: Students list numbers near n rather than testing divisibility, or confuse factors with multiples.
candidates.note: Lists multiples or neighbouring integers instead of divisors, giving a specific wrong factor list or count.

candidates.failure_mode: Students say 1 is prime or think every odd number is prime.
candidates.note: Counts 1 as prime or every odd as prime, producing specific wrong classifications and counts.

candidates.failure_mode: Students double-count factor pairs or stop too early before reaching square root.
candidates.note: Double-counts a pair or stops before sqrt(n), so the factor count is off by a determinate amount.

candidates.failure_mode: Students list factors correctly but fail to notice the square-root factor is counted once.
candidates.note: Counts the square-root factor twice, turning an odd factor count into an even one.

candidates.failure_mode: Students brute-force every integer and miss the structural shortcut that 4=2², 9=3², 25=5², etc.
candidates.note: Brute force is slow but reaches the right answer; the missing structural shortcut costs time, not correctness.

candidates.failure_mode: Students list factor pairs without using parity to eliminate impossible sum choices quickly, or they incorrectly assume an even product implies both numbers are even.
candidates.note: Infers from an even product that both factors are even, eliminating the wrong candidate pairs and yielding a specific wrong sum.

candidates.failure_mode: Students create equations with two variables but do not restrict x and y to integer factor pairs, leading to unnecessary algebra or impossible cases.
candidates.note: Not restricting to integer factor pairs adds algebra and dead ends rather than producing a characteristic wrong value.

candidates.failure_mode: Students divide the wrong way because they ignore whether the answer should be hours per room or rooms per hour.
candidates.note: Divides in the wrong direction, returning the reciprocal of the asked rate.

candidates.failure_mode: Students can compute total work but cannot answer per-item or per-time questions.
candidates.note: Stated as an inability to answer per-unit questions rather than a procedure. Borderline: reporting the total where the per-unit rate is asked would be an executable substitution.

candidates.failure_mode: Students use 2-foot side length as if it covers 2 square feet instead of 4 square feet.
candidates.note: Uses the linear measure as the area measure, e.g. 2 ft treated as 2 sq ft instead of 4.

candidates.failure_mode: Students convert hours to minutes but forget that area conversion squares the conversion factor.
candidates.note: Omits squaring the conversion factor for area, so the result is off by that factor.

candidates.failure_mode: Students combine unlike terms such as 5x and 5x² or fail to combine 5x+2x.
candidates.note: Combines 5x with 5x^2, or leaves 5x + 2x uncombined, giving a specific wrong expression.

candidates.failure_mode: Students substitute into only one occurrence or forget parentheses around negative numbers.
candidates.note: Substitutes into one occurrence only, or drops parentheses around a negative, giving a specific wrong evaluation.

candidates.failure_mode: Students freeze because multiple letters appear, or divide by the wrong symbol, or do not know what “in terms of” means.
candidates.note: Divides by the wrong symbol when solving for a named variable, giving a specific wrong rearranged form.

candidates.failure_mode: Students evaluate the prompt correctly but cannot match it to an answer choice written in equivalent form.
candidates.note: The value is computed correctly; the failure is not recognising the equivalent form among the options.

candidates.failure_mode: Students multiply only some terms or forget that every term on both sides must be multiplied.
candidates.note: Multiplies only some terms by the LCD, leaving the untouched terms unscaled.

candidates.failure_mode: Students add random x and y variables or translate operations in the wrong order.
candidates.note: Translates the operations in the wrong order (e.g. '5 less than x' as 5 - x), giving a specific wrong equation; requires reading the prose.

candidates.failure_mode: Students know inequality symbols but cannot read them from a picture, or reverse endpoint inclusions.
candidates.note: Reverses the endpoint inclusion or direction read off the picture, giving a specific wrong inequality.

candidates.failure_mode: Students pick random sides rather than corresponding sides, or confuse similarity with congruence.
candidates.note: Pairs non-corresponding sides from the diagram, giving a specific wrong ratio.

candidates.failure_mode: Students memorize the slope formula but cannot see rise/run in a graph, or swap x and y changes.
candidates.note: Swaps the x and y changes when reading rise/run, returning the reciprocal slope; the read is graphical.

candidates.failure_mode: Students can execute a procedure only after being told which procedure to use; they fail when the structure is implicit.
candidates.note: Recognising which procedure a problem calls for is a strategy-selection skill; failing it stalls the student rather than producing a wrong value.

candidates.failure_mode: Students waste time deriving when substitution into choices would be faster.
candidates.note: A time/method-choice skill; not using backsolving costs time and produces no characteristic wrong value.

candidates.failure_mode: Students compute blindly and accept answers that have impossible units or magnitude.
candidates.note: A self-monitoring skill; failing to sanity-check lets other errors through rather than generating one.

candidates.failure_mode: Students try to hold geometry verbally in working memory and miss the helpful line/shape.
candidates.note: A working-memory offloading strategy; not drawing the diagram blocks progress rather than yielding a wrong number.

candidates.failure_mode: Students apply their favorite method to every problem even when another pathway would be faster or safer.
candidates.note: A method-selection skill; the default method is usually still correct, only slower or riskier.
